steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting a new DID Method built on the IOTA Tangle and its integration into OpenSSL. Start by explaining the Self-Sovereign Identity stack layer by layer (DIDs, DID Methods, Verifiable Credentials, the Triangle-of-Trust), then say what the paper focuses on and list its contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) and the SSI stack
- Layer 1: DLT, DIDs, DID Documents, DID Methods
- Layers 2 and 3: secure channel, Verifiable Credentials
- Digital identity in SSI
- Triangle-of-Trust roles: Holder, Issuer, Verifier
- VC / VP structure
- This paper: OTT DID Method on the IOTA Tangle, OpenSSL integration, contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- SSI
  - decentralized digital identity paradigm (cite); humans and things fully control identity data
  - stack in Fig. 1, new model for trusted digital interactions
- Layer 1
  - any DLT as Root-of-Trust (RoT) for identity data; DLTs distributed immutable storage by design (cite)
  - DID (cite): globally unique identity to verify a subject
  - URI form did:method-name:method-specific-id; method-name = DID Method, method-specific-id = pointer to DID Document on DLT
  - DIDs associate subject with DID Document (cite)
  - DID Method (cite): software to interact with specific ledger
  - W3C recommendation (cite): primitives (i) create: key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}), DID Document with public key, store on ledger (ii) resolve: retrieve DID Document, verify DID (iii) update: new DID + Document, revoke previous (iv) revoke: immutable evidence on ledger
  - ledger-specific; upper layers independent of ledger
- Layers 2-3
  - Layer 2: DIDs + DID Documents for secure channel between two peers; prove ownership of sk_{id} bound to pk_{id}
  - Layer 2 starts authentication, Layer 3 finalizes it + authorization via Verifiable Credentials (cite)
  - VCs: secure, machine verifiable; unforgeable document with more identity characteristics; signatures -> tamper-evident
- Digital identity
  - key pair + DID + DID Document + at least one VC
  - decentralized: no single authority provides all or can fully revoke
  - multiple VCs from different issuers
- Triangle-of-Trust (Fig. 1)
  - Holder: has VCs, makes Verifiable Presentation (VP) to request service/resource from Verifier
  - Issuer: asserts claims about subject, creates VC, issues to Holders; multiple Issuers
  - Verifier: receives VP, checks Issuer signature on VC and Holder signature on VP, grants access
- VC / VP
  - metadata (context, ID, type, Issuer, issuance and expiration dates), claims in credentialSubject field
  - Issuer signature -> unforgeable, verifiable
  - VP = envelope of VC signed by Holder
  - Issuers handle VC revocation for cryptographic integrity and status change (cite)
  - any ecosystem of trustable interactions on top
- This paper
  - Layer 1; novel DID Method Over-The-Tangle (OTT)
  - on IOTA Tangle (cite): DLT, feeless transactions, attach any data
  - contributions (i) design + implementation of OTT (ii) statistically relevant performance results in real world settings
  - future: TLS handshake with DIDs and DID Documents, interoperable with public key certificates
  - (iii) logic in OpenSSL (cite) for agile integration of DID Methods via novel DID Provider; Provider = unit of code with implementations of operations for algorithms (cite); collects DID Methods, available to LibSSL (TLS handshake); DID Operation defines templates for Create, Resolve, Update, Revoke
  - (iv) easy procedure to add other DID Methods

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is a paradigm for decentralized digital identity that gives both human beings and things full control over the data they use to build and prove their identity. The whole SSI stack, shown in Fig. 1, makes possible a new model for trusted digital interactions.

Layer 1 is implemented with any Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), which acts as the Root-of-Trust (RoT) for identity data. This is because DLTs are by design distributed and immutable means of storage. A Decentralized IDentifier (DID) is a globally unique identity that is designed to verify a subject. DIDs are Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) of the form did:method-name:method-specific-id, where method-name is the name of the DID Method that is used to interact with the DLT, and method-specific-id is the pointer to the DID Document that is stored on the DLT. So DIDs associate a DID subject with a DID Document so that there can be trustable interactions with that subject. The DID Method is a software implementation for interacting with a specific ledger technology. According to the W3C recommendation, a DID Method has to provide the primitives (i) to create the DID, which means generating a key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}) for authentication, generating the corresponding DID Document that contains the public key of the pair, and storing the DID Document in the ledger at the method-specific-id the DID points to, (ii) to resolve a DID, which means retrieving the DID Document from the method-specific-id on the ledger that the DID points to and verifying that the DID is valid, (iii) to update the DID, which means generating a new DID and DID Document and revoking the previous one, and (iv) to revoke a DID, which means providing immutable evidence on the ledger that the owner of the DID has revoked it. The implementation of the DID Method is specific to the ledger, and this makes the upper layers independent of the specific ledger technology.

Layer 2 uses DIDs and DID Documents to set up a secure channel between two peers. In principle both peers prove that they own the private key sk_{id} bound to the public key pk_{id} in the DID Document stored on the ledger. Layer 2 uses DID technology (i.e. the security foundation of the SSI stack) to start the authentication procedure, and Layer 3 finishes it and handles authorization to services and resources using Verifiable Credentials. VCs are secure digital credentials that machines can verify. A VC is an unforgeable digital document that contains more characteristics of the digital identity of a peer than just a key pair, a DID and the related DID Document. Because digital signatures are added, VCs are tamper-evident and trustworthy.

The key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}), a DID, the related DID Document and at least one VC together form the digital identity in the SSI world. This way of composing the digital identity reflects that SSI is decentralized. No authority gives a peer all the components of the identity and no authority can completely revoke the identity of a peer. Also, a peer can add to its identity with multiple VCs from different issuers.

- Triangle-of-Trust (Layer 3, Fig. 1), three roles
  - Holder: has VCs, generates Verifiable Presentation (VP) to request service/resource from Verifier
  - Issuer: asserts claims, creates VC, issues to Holders; multiple Issuers
  - Verifier: receives VP, verifies Issuer signature on VC + Holder signature on VP, grants access
- VC / VP
  - metadata (context, ID, type, Issuer of the VC, issuance and expiration dates); claims in credentialSubject field
  - Issuer signature -> unforgeable, verifiable; VP = envelope of VC signed by Holder
  - Issuers responsible for VC revocation (cryptographic integrity, status change)
  - any ecosystem of trustable interactions on top of three layers
- This paper
  - Layer 1, novel DID Method Over-The-Tangle (OTT), on IOTA Tangle (feeless transactions, any data)
  - (i) design + implementation of OTT (ii) statistically relevant performance results, real world settings
  - future: TLS handshake with DIDs/DID Documents, interoperable with public key certificates
  - (iii) OpenSSL logic, DID Provider; Provider definition; collects DID Methods for LibSSL; DID Operation templates for Create, Resolve, Update, Revoke
  - (iv) easy procedure to add other DID Methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is a paradigm for decentralized digital identity that gives both human beings and things full control over the data they use to build and prove their identity. The whole SSI stack, shown in Fig. 1, makes possible a new model for trusted digital interactions.

Layer 1 is implemented with any Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), which acts as the Root-of-Trust (RoT) for identity data. This is because DLTs are by design distributed and immutable means of storage. A Decentralized IDentifier (DID) is a globally unique identity that is designed to verify a subject. DIDs are Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) of the form did:method-name:method-specific-id, where method-name is the name of the DID Method that is used to interact with the DLT, and method-specific-id is the pointer to the DID Document that is stored on the DLT. So DIDs associate a DID subject with a DID Document so that there can be trustable interactions with that subject. The DID Method is a software implementation for interacting with a specific ledger technology. According to the W3C recommendation, a DID Method has to provide the primitives (i) to create the DID, which means generating a key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}) for authentication, generating the corresponding DID Document that contains the public key of the pair, and storing the DID Document in the ledger at the method-specific-id the DID points to, (ii) to resolve a DID, which means retrieving the DID Document from the method-specific-id on the ledger that the DID points to and verifying that the DID is valid, (iii) to update the DID, which means generating a new DID and DID Document and revoking the previous one, and (iv) to revoke a DID, which means providing immutable evidence on the ledger that the owner of the DID has revoked it. The implementation of the DID Method is specific to the ledger, and this makes the upper layers independent of the specific ledger technology.

Layer 2 uses DIDs and DID Documents to set up a secure channel between two peers. In principle both peers prove that they own the private key sk_{id} bound to the public key pk_{id} in the DID Document stored on the ledger. Layer 2 uses DID technology (i.e. the security foundation of the SSI stack) to start the authentication procedure, and Layer 3 finishes it and handles authorization to services and resources using Verifiable Credentials. VCs are secure digital credentials that machines can verify. A VC is an unforgeable digital document that contains more characteristics of the digital identity of a peer than just a key pair, a DID and the related DID Document. Because digital signatures are added, VCs are tamper-evident and trustworthy.

The key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}), a DID, the related DID Document and at least one VC together form the digital identity in the SSI world. This way of composing the digital identity reflects that SSI is decentralized. No authority gives a peer all the components of the identity and no authority can completely revoke the identity of a peer. Also, a peer can add to its identity with multiple VCs from different issuers.

Layer 3 works according to the Triangle-of-Trust shown in Fig. 1. There are three different roles:

- Holder is the peer that has one or more VCs and that generates a Verifiable Presentation (VP) to request a service or a resource from a Verifier;

- Issuer is the peer that asserts claims about a subject, creates a VC from these claims, and issues the VC to the Holders. There can be multiple Issuers.

- Verifier is the peer that receives a VP from the Holder and verifies the two signatures, the one made by the Issuer on the VC and the one made by the Holder on the VP, before it grants him/her access to a service or a resource based on the claims.

A VC has metadata that describes properties of the credential (e.g. context, ID, type, Issuer of the VC, issuance and expiration dates) and, most importantly, the claims about the identity of the subject in the credentialSubject field. The Issuer makes the digital signature so that the VC is an unforgeable and verifiable digital document. The Holder asks the Verifier for access to services and/or resources by presenting a VP. A VP is built as an envelope of the VC issued by an Issuer, with the signature made by the Holder. Issuers are also responsible for revoking VCs, both for cryptographic integrity and for status change purposes. On top of these three layers it is possible to build any ecosystem of trustable interactions among human beings and things.

This paper is about Layer 1 of the SSI stack and presents for the first time a new DID Method called Over-The-Tangle (OTT). OTT works directly on top of the IOTA Tangle, which is a DLT that offers feeless transactions to attach any type of data to the structure of the distributed ledger. The paper gives the following new contributions: (i) design and implementation of the OTT DID Method and (ii) statistically relevant results on the overall performance of the solution in real world settings. Then, based on these results, the paper discusses some future perspectives and proposes to work on designing a Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake that uses DIDs and DID Documents while keeping interoperability with public key certificates. As a first step toward this, the paper gives two more contributions, (iii) design and implementation of the logic in OpenSSL for agile integration of DID Methods through a new DID Provider. A Provider, in OpenSSL terms, is a unit of code that provides one or more implementations for various operations for diverse algorithms that one might want to perform; in this work the Provider collects a series of DID Methods and makes them available to LibSSL, a sub-module of OpenSSL that implements the TLS handshake; this new DID Operation universally defines the templates (i.e. inputs and return values) for the DID Method functions Create, Resolve, Update, and Revoke, and (iv) an easy to follow procedure to add other DID Methods in an agile way, which opens the way for further adoption of the solution.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) [1] is a decentralized digital identity paradigm that gives both human beings and things full control over the data they use to build and prove their identity. The overall SSI stack, depicted in Fig. 1, enables a new model for trusted digital interactions.

Layer 1 is implemented by means of any Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) acting as the Root-of-Trust (RoT) for identity data, since DLTs are distributed immutable means of storage by design [2]. A Decentralized IDentifier (DID) [3] is a globally unique identity designed to verify a subject. DIDs are Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) in the form did:method-name:method-specific-id, where method-name is the name of the DID Method used to interact with the DLT and method-specific-id is the pointer to the DID Document stored on the DLT. DIDs thus associate a DID subject with a DID Document [3] to enable trustable interactions with that subject. The DID Method [3,4] is a software implementation for interacting with a specific ledger technology. In accordance with the W3C recommendation [3], a DID Method must provide the primitives (i) to create the DID, that is, generate a key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}) for authentication purposes and the corresponding DID Document containing the public key of the pair, and store the DID Document into the ledger at the method-specific-id pointed to by the DID, (ii) to resolve a DID, that is, retrieve the DID Document from the method-specific-id on the ledger pointed to by the DID and verify the validity of the DID, (iii) to update the DID, that is, generate a new DID and corresponding DID Document while revoking the previous one, and (iv) to revoke a DID, that is, provide immutable evidence on the ledger that the DID has been revoked by its owner. The DID Method implementation is ledger-specific, which makes the upper layers independent from the specific ledger technology.

Layer 2 makes use of DIDs and DID Documents to establish a secure channel between two peers. In principle, both peers prove ownership of the private key sk_{id} bound to the public key pk_{id} in the DID Document stored on the ledger. While Layer 2 leverages DID technology (i.e. the security foundation of the SSI stack) to begin the authentication procedure, Layer 3 finalizes it and deals with authorization to services and resources by means of Verifiable Credentials [5]. VCs are secure and machine verifiable digital credentials. A VC is an unforgeable digital document that contains further characteristics of a peer's digital identity beyond a simple key pair, a DID and the related DID Document. Digital signatures make VCs tamper-evident and trustworthy.

The combination of the key pair (sk_{id},pk_{id}), a DID, the related DID Document and at least one VC forms the digital identity in the SSI world. This composition reflects the decentralized nature of SSI: no authority provides all the components of the identity to a peer, and no authority is able to completely revoke the identity of a peer. Moreover, a peer can enrich its identity with multiple VCs issued by different issuers.

Layer 3 works in accordance with the Triangle-of-Trust depicted in Fig. 1, in which three different roles coexist:

- Holder is the peer that possesses one or more VCs and generates a Verifiable Presentation (VP) to request a service or a resource from a Verifier;

- Issuer is the peer that asserts claims about a subject, creates a VC from these claims, and issues the VC to the Holders. Multiple Issuers can coexist.

- Verifier is the peer that receives a VP from the Holder and verifies the two signatures, made by the Issuer on the VC and by the Holder on the VP, before granting him/her access to a service or a resource based on the claims.

A VC contains the metadata describing properties of the credential (e.g. context, ID, type, Issuer of the VC, issuance and expiration dates) and, most importantly, the claims about the identity of the subject in the credentialSubject field. The Issuer makes the digital signature that turns the VC into an unforgeable and verifiable digital document. The Holder requests access to services and/or resources from the Verifier by presenting a VP, built as an envelope of the VC issued by an Issuer and signed by the Holder. Issuers are also responsible for VC revocation for cryptographic integrity and status change purposes [5]. On top of these three layers, any ecosystem of trustable interactions among human beings and things can be built.

This paper focuses on Layer 1 of the SSI stack and presents for the first time a novel DID Method called Over-The-Tangle (OTT). OTT works directly on top of the IOTA Tangle [6], a DLT offering feeless transactions to attach any type of data to the structure of the distributed ledger. The paper provides the following novel contributions: (i) design and implementation of the OTT DID Method and (ii) statistically relevant results on the overall performance of the solution in real world settings. Supported by these results, the paper then discusses some future perspectives and proposes to work on the design of a Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake making use of DIDs and DID Documents while maintaining interoperability with public key certificates. As a first step toward this objective, the paper provides two further contributions: (iii) design and implementation of the logic in OpenSSL [7] for agile integration of DID Methods through a novel DID Provider. A Provider, in OpenSSL terms, is a unit of code that provides one or more implementations for various operations for diverse algorithms that one might want to perform [8]; in this work, the Provider collects a series of DID Methods and makes them available to LibSSL, the sub-module of OpenSSL implementing the TLS handshake; this novel DID Operation universally defines the templates (i.e. inputs and return values) for the DID Method functions Create, Resolve, Update, and Revoke; and (iv) an easy to follow procedure to add other DID Methods in an agile fashion, opening the way for further adoption of the solution.
